idea: Seed: port of the production MLP + train_ann.

The parent early-stops and schedules LR on a random validation split, but the test set is temporally held out — a random split lets the model validate on rows interleaved with training cycles, so "best val" rewards memorizing time-local structure and picks a checkpoint that overfits temporally. Since rows are flattened cycle-by-cycle in time order, I replace the random split with a contiguous tail split: the last 10% of rows becomes validation, mimicking the harness's later-cycles holdout. Early stopping and ReduceLROnPlateau now optimize exactly the quantity being scored (forward-in-time generalization), which should raise held-out R^2 with zero extra compute. Everything else is unchanged to isolate the effect.

The parent's masked MSE is computed on raw m/s targets, so the component with larger variance (v: r2_v 0.215 vs r2_u 0.125) soaks up most of the gradient budget while u is under-fit — yet the score is the unweighted mean of the two R²s, and R² is scale-invariant per component. I standardize each target component by its own nan-aware mean/std, train the joint head in normalized space (masked MSE now weights u and v equally in units of their own variance, i.e. it directly optimizes average R²), and un-standardize predictions at the end. Everything else — architecture, random validation split (the temporal tail split of gen001 lost), optimizer, schedule — is unchanged to isolate the effect; the expected gain is a rebalanced u without sacrificing much v.

The parent's temporal validation improved r2_u but collapsed r2_v, likely because holding out the last 10% of rows removes the training data closest in time to the test cycles — exactly the samples most informative about the future regime. I keep the temporal tail for early stopping (it selects for forward-in-time generalization), but after restoring the best checkpoint I add a short low-LR "recency fine-tune" over the full dataset — tail included, with the tail epochs run last — so the model adapts to the most recent conditions before predicting the held-out future, recovering the v-component signal without abandoning temporal model selection.

Crossover of the parent with the current best: keep the parent's per-component target standardization (it makes the pooled masked MSE weight u and v equally in variance units, matching the mean-R² objective), but replace its random validation split — which selects for interleaved memorization, not the forward-in-time generalization the temporal test split measures — with gen001_02's proven scheme: hold out the last 10% of rows as a contiguous temporal tail for early stopping and LR scheduling, then after restoring the best checkpoint run a short low-LR recency fine-tune over the full dataset in oldest→newest block order so the samples nearest the test cycles shape the final weights. The temporal scheme was worth +0.114 fitness over the seed on its own; the target standardization should now help rather than hurt because model selection is no longer rewarding the random-split optimum.

The parent's single MLP trained in 79s, leaving budget on the table, and single-seed deep nets on noisy geophysical targets carry high variance — averaging independently initialized members is the most reliable variance-reduction available. I keep the parent's proven recipe (temporal-tail validation, raw-m/s masked MSE, recency fine-tune) completely unchanged and wrap it in a budget-aware seed ensemble: up to 3 members trained with different seeds on staggered slices of the wall clock (the first member gets half the budget so it alone is at least parent-strength if time is tight), with predictions averaged in m/s. Ensemble averaging cannot hurt expected R² relative to a typical single member and usually adds several points on temporally shifted test data because the members' regime-extrapolation errors are partly decorrelated.

The parent's weakness is that its MLP must learn the full u,v field from scratch and its random validation split selects for interpolation (history shows temporal-tail validation is what fixed this lineage). I make one structural change: two-stage residual learning. A closed-form ridge regression (per component, masked, on the standardized features) is fit first as a linear baseline — it captures the dominant, physically-grounded linear geostrophy→velocity relationship and, being linear, extrapolates stably to unseen later cycles. The MLP then trains only on the residuals, with the parent's per-component standardization now applied to residuals so u and v get equal gradient weight in variance units. I also import the leaderboard-proven temporal-tail validation split in place of the random split, since keeping the known-bad selection rule would mask the residual scheme's effect. Predictions are ridge baseline + de-standardized residual net, so even if the net adds little on shifted regimes, the linear part sets a much higher floor than the parent's 0.13.

The parent ensemble must spend its early epochs re-learning the strong linear relation between the geostrophic-velocity features and (u, v) — and SGD on 1M noisy rows fits that linear part imperfectly and differently per seed, which especially hurts the weaker u component. I add a closed-form masked ridge-regression baseline fit on the full standardized training set (per component, exact, deterministic, ~seconds), and train the same temporally-validated MLP ensemble on the residuals. The linear/geostrophic signal is now captured exactly on all data with zero optimization noise, the MLPs concentrate capacity on the nonlinear/ageostrophic correction, and the final prediction is ridge + ensemble-mean residual — a guaranteed-at-least-linear predictor that should lift r2_u without disturbing what already works for v.

The score is the mean of per-component R², but the parent trains with a plain masked MSE, which implicitly weights u and v by their raw residual variance — v's larger, easier-to-reduce errors dominate the gradient while u (r2_u 0.244 vs r2_v 0.368) is under-served. Since mean R² = 1 − mean(MSE_c/Var_c), the loss that exactly matches the metric is an inverse-variance-weighted MSE. I keep the parent's ridge-baseline + residual-MLP ensemble untouched and make one change: compute each component's masked residual variance after the ridge fit, scale that component's loss contribution by var_mean/var_c (clipped for safety), and use this metric-aligned weighting in training, validation early-stopping, and the recency fine-tune. This redirects capacity toward u, which has the most headroom, and makes model selection pick checkpoints that optimize the actual score. I also fix the loss to weight squared errors linearly (the parent's form squares the mask, which was harmless only because the mask was binary).

Both top candidates show the ridge+residual-MLP recipe works, but r2_u (≈0.245) still lags r2_v (≈0.365) badly. On the US west coast the u (cross-shore) component is largely wind-driven Ekman flow, and wind stress is *quadratic* in wind speed — yet the module only exposes era5_u, era5_v linearly, so the exact ridge stage cannot capture the stress response at all and the MLP must burn capacity rediscovering it from stencil copies. I append four physically-motivated nonlinear columns computed from per-row stencil-block means of the raw features: wind speed |W|, pseudo-stress components era5_u·|W| and era5_v·|W|, and geostrophic current speed (nonlinear advection proxy). These feed both the closed-form ridge (which can now fit the Ekman/stress relation deterministically on all 1M rows) and the residual MLPs, targeting the u headroom while leaving the proven training recipe (temporal validation, metric-aligned weighting, budgeted seed ensemble, recency fine-tune) untouched.

The parent's single MLP scores only 0.14 while the ridge+residual-MLP family sits at ~0.30, and the biggest measured jump in the whole history came from adding a closed-form masked ridge baseline (gen002_02): the exact linear fit captures the dominant geostrophic signal on all 1M rows with zero SGD noise, and the network only has to learn the nonlinear/ageostrophic correction. I make exactly that one change to the parent — fit a deterministic per-component masked ridge on the standardized features (seconds, chunked normal equations), train the parent's unchanged temporally-validated MLP on the residuals, and predict ridge + residual. This guarantees an at-least-linear predictor (the parent can currently underperform its own linear part, which its anomalous r2_v of 0.12 suggests), shrinks the target variance the MLP must model, and should lift both components toward the 0.30 frontier while keeping the module simple enough for later mutations (ensembling, loss shaping) to build on.

Both top candidates train each ensemble member to a single point estimate of the weights: the raw last-batch SGD iterate (or the single best-epoch snapshot), which on 1M noisy geophysical rows bounces around the loss basin — that iterate noise is exactly why the seed ensemble helps. I add an exponential moving average (EMA) of the weights (decay 0.999, ~5-epoch horizon) maintained during each member's training: validation, early stopping, and the returned predictor all use the EMA weights, and the recency fine-tune keeps a shorter-horizon EMA (0.995) so the oldest→newest sweep's recency tilt survives but its last-batch jitter doesn't. EMA is a free ensemble-along-the-trajectory for each member — it consistently improves held-out performance for noisy regression at near-zero cost (one extra ~120k-param copy), so it should smooth every member's contribution and lift both r2_u and r2_v without touching the ridge baseline, weighting, or budget logic that already work.

The parent imputes NaN stencil cells with 0 — the post-standardization feature mean — so a swath-edge row whose neighbors are padding is indistinguishable from an interior row whose neighbors genuinely sit at average conditions. Both the ridge baseline and the residual MLP therefore fit a systematically biased map at swath edges (a large fraction of rows in a 3×3 stencil over narrow swaths), and can't down-weight fabricated neighbor values. I make one change: append binary validity-indicator columns for every input column that is actually sometimes-missing (constant always-valid columns are filtered out to avoid dead inputs), and feed the augmented matrix through the otherwise-unchanged pipeline — ridge, residual MLP ensemble, temporal validation, and recency fine-tune all see the indicators. The ridge can learn closed-form per-pattern offset corrections and the MLP can gate stencil features on their validity, which should recover accuracy on edge rows and lift both r2_u and r2_v without touching anything that already works; the cost is only a modestly wider input (~≤2× d), negligible on this budget.

Both top candidates show r2_u (~0.24) lagging r2_v (~0.37), and on the US West Coast the u (cross-shore) component is dominated by wind-driven Ekman flow rather than geostrophy — but wind forcing enters the ocean through wind STRESS, which scales quadratically (τ ∝ |U|U), a relation neither the linear ridge nor easily the small MLP can recover from raw era5_u/era5_v columns. I append physics-derived wind-stress features (τ_u = u·|U|, τ_v = v·|U|, and wind speed |U|) computed per stencil cell from the known feature-major layout (9 base features × k² cells, with a shape guard so the module degrades gracefully). The ridge baseline can now capture the Ekman response in closed form on all data — directly targeting the weak u component — while everything that measurably worked (ridge+residual MLP ensemble, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, missingness indicators) is left untouched.

The parent trains its residual MLP with plain masked MSE, but the ridge residuals it fits are exactly the part of the signal dominated by heavy-tailed noise: HFR-derived velocities carry large geometric-dilution and interference outliers (worst for the cross-shore u component), and ageostrophic events produce rare huge residuals that MSE gradients chase at the expense of the predictable bulk. I make one change: train (and recency-fine-tune) with a masked Huber loss whose per-component delta is set to one standard deviation of that component's post-ridge residual, so typical errors keep their exact MSE gradient while outlier rows get linearly-clipped gradients instead of quadratic dominance. Crucially, validation early-stopping still uses plain masked MSE — the quantity the R² metric actually measures — so robust optimization improves the fit of the predictable signal while checkpoint selection stays metric-aligned. Everything else (ridge baseline, temporal split, 3-seed ensemble, budget slicing) is untouched.

The lagging component is u — cross-shore flow on the US West Coast, which is dominated by wind-driven Ekman/upwelling dynamics that are nonlinear in the wind (stress ∝ |W|·W) and by frontal ageostrophic motion — none of which a linear ridge or an MLP fed only raw stencil copies captures easily. I append nine physics-derived, stencil-ordering-invariant features computed NaN-aware from the known feature-major 3×3 stencil layout: wind speed and quadratic-drag wind-stress components (|W|Wu, |W|Wv), geostrophic and ageostrophic current speeds, and within-stencil standard deviations of SSHA, SST, ugos and vgos (frontal/shear activity proxies). These feed both the closed-form ridge and the residual MLP ensemble unchanged, so the proven gen004_01 recipe is untouched; the new columns inject exactly the nonlinear Ekman/frontal signal that should lift r2_u without disturbing v.

The lineage's best change so far is gen004_01's masked-Huber training (metric-aligned MSE checkpointing kept), so I keep that and make one new change: replace the ensemble's naive equal-weight average with per-component ridge stacking fit on the temporal validation tail — the data most exchangeable with the held-out later cycles. Each member's residual predictions on the tail are captured at its early-stopped checkpoint (before the recency fine-tune touches the tail, limiting leakage), and I solve a tiny closed-form ridge for combination weights over [members, a linear-baseline adjustment, an intercept], with scale-aware shrinkage toward the parent's defaults (equal member weights, lin weight 1, zero intercept). This lets the combiner rebalance toward whichever members and baseline amplitude actually generalize forward in time — weights are fit per component, so the lagging u channel gets its own mix — while shrinkage plus a finiteness/blow-up fallback bounds the downside at parent behavior.

The parent shares the ridge+residual skeleton of the best lineage but trains a single raw-SGD net, and it scored far below gen004_01, whose Huber training, MSE-aligned checkpointing, temporal validation, seed ensemble, and recency fine-tune all measurably worked — so I keep that full recipe and make one change: maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) of the MLP weights (dynamic decay warming up to 0.999) and use the EMA weights for validation, early-stopping checkpoints, the fine-tune starting point, and final prediction. A single SGD endpoint is a noisy sample from the tail of the trajectory; the EMA is a temporal ensemble along the trajectory that sits in a flatter region of the loss surface, and flat minima are exactly what generalize under the distribution shift of a temporally held-out test split. It also makes checkpoint selection lower-variance (the validation curve of the EMA is far smoother, so patience-based stopping picks a genuinely better model rather than a lucky epoch) — at the cost of one cheap parameter copy per step for a ~120k-parameter net.

The parent added tail-fitted stacking on top of gen004_01's plain seed average, and the component scores reveal it is a mixed bet: versus gen004_01, stacking lifted v (0.361→0.370) but crushed u (0.261→0.240) — exactly the component whose HFR-derived tail residuals are noisiest, so its tiny ridge fit overfits tail noise that does not transfer forward. I make one change: per-component inner selection between the stacked combiner and the plain average. The chronological tail is split in half; stacking weights are fit on the older half and must beat the plain member average's MSE on the newer (most test-like) half by a small margin before being adopted — winners are then refit on the full tail, losers fall back to the gen004_01-style average. This keeps stacking where it demonstrably generalizes (v) and reverts it where it demonstrably hurts (u), so the candidate should combine the parent's best r2_v with the inspiration's best r2_u. Everything else (ridge baseline, Huber training with MSE checkpointing, recency fine-tune, budget slicing) is untouched.

The lineage's gains have all come from removing SGD noise from the final predictor (exact ridge for the linear part, seed-averaging for the residual nets), so I push the same lever inside each member: maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) of the MLP weights during training (decay 0.999 with a warmup schedule so early EMA tracks the live net), validate and checkpoint the EMA weights instead of the raw ones, and continue the EMA through the recency fine-tune so the returned member is the smoothed model. Weight averaging along the SGD trajectory is a cheap, well-established generalization booster (SWA/EMA): it lands the weights in a flatter region of the loss surface and suppresses the batch-to-batch jitter that plain last-iterate/best-iterate checkpointing inherits — which should especially help the noisier u component, and it costs only one extra tiny forward-model copy, so ensemble size and the time budget are untouched.

Both generation-5 EMA candidates (this parent and gen005_02) collapsed to an identical 0.1930 — the ridge-only score — meaning the EMA machinery zeroed out the MLP's residual contribution, so I revert that change entirely and rebuild on the best verified skeleton, gen004_01 (0.3109). My one new change is physics-motivated feature engineering aimed at the lagging u component: cross-shore flow on the US West Coast is Ekman/upwelling dynamics forced by wind STRESS, which is quadratic in wind speed (τ ∝ |U|·U), but the module currently offers only raw linear era5_u/era5_v. I append, per stencil cell, wind speed |U| and the two pseudo-stress components |U|·u10 and |U|·v10 (27 new columns), computed before standardization so both the closed-form ridge and the residual MLP see them. The ridge can now represent the linear stress→Ekman-current map directly (including its 90° rotation), and the MLP no longer has to synthesize a quadratic from scratch — a targeted lift for r2_u with negligible cost, guarded to activate only for the known 81-column layout.

I rebuild on the strongest verified skeleton (gen005_03, 0.3115 = gen004_01's masked-Huber training + wind-stress augmentation) and make one new change: generalize the stress-style feature augmentation from the wind to the geostrophic current itself. The surface-to-subsurface velocity transfer is not linear in the surface current — vertical shear, bottom/interfacial drag (∝|U|·U), and Ekman-layer attenuation all depend on current speed — yet the module gives the ridge and MLP only the raw linear ugos/vgos columns. I append, per stencil cell, the geostrophic speed |Ug| and the pseudo-stress components |Ug|·ug and |Ug|·vg (27 more columns, 81→135 total with the wind block), computed before standardization so the closed-form ridge can directly represent speed-dependent attenuation and rotation of the geostrophic→subsurface map, and the residual MLP starts from a richer basis instead of synthesizing the quadratic itself. This mirrors the exact mechanism of the lineage's best verified gain, now aimed at the dominant (geostrophic) part of the signal that drives both components, with negligible compute/memory cost and the same 81-column layout guard.

I build on the strongest verified program (gen006_00, 0.3223: masked-Huber residual training + wind pseudo-stress + geostrophic pseudo-stress) and make one new change: recency-weighted training of the residual MLP. The test split is temporally held out, and the lineage's recency fine-tune already showed that late samples matter more — but the main training loop still treats a row from cycle 474 as exactly as informative about the test cycles as one from cycle 570, even though mesoscale eddy positions and the seasonal upwelling regime decorrelate over weeks. I fold an exponential time-decay importance weight (newest row weight 1.0, oldest ≈0.37, tau = the training span) into the Huber loss mask for both the main loop and the fine-tune, while leaving the closed-form ridge unweighted (it captures the time-stationary linear physics on all data) and leaving validation/early-stopping as unweighted MSE on the temporal tail (the selection criterion must stay an unbiased proxy for the test metric). This shifts the MLP's capacity toward the ocean state actually adjacent to the held-out cycles at zero extra compute, and only for the residual component where the non-stationarity lives.

I build on the strongest verified program (gen006_00, 0.3223) rather than the parent, since the parent's recency weighting measurably lost ground (0.3210), and make one new change: component-balanced training. The score is the mean of R²(u) and R²(v) — a scale-invariant average — but the shared-trunk MLP is trained on raw masked Huber in m/s units, so whichever component has the larger post-ridge residual variance dominates every gradient step. The lineage's scores show a persistent imbalance (r2_u ≈ 0.27 vs r2_v ≈ 0.37): u is systematically under-served by the loss. I weight each component's loss by its inverse residual variance (1/δ_c²), normalized to mean 1 so the overall gradient magnitude — and thus the tuned LR/schedule — is unchanged, and apply the same weights to the validation MSE so checkpoint selection optimizes the same balanced quantity the metric measures. This shifts shared capacity toward the harder u component exactly in proportion to how the metric values it, at zero compute cost and with no structural risk to the verified skeleton.

I build on the strongest verified program (gen006_02, 0.3253: component-balanced masked-Huber residual training on top of the exact ridge with wind pseudo-stress and current-speed physics features) and make one new change following the lineage's most reliably rewarded pattern — physics-motivated feature augmentation for the ridge+MLP: stencil-spread features. For each of the 9 base features I append the NaN-aware standard deviation across its 3x3 stencil cells (135 → 144 columns). This is a genuinely NEW nonlinear signal: any linear combination of stencil cells (gradients, vorticity, strain) is already representable by the ridge, but the spread — local front strength / mesoscale roughness of SSH, geostrophic velocity, wind, SST — is not, and it is exactly the regime variable oceanography says modulates the surface→subsurface transfer (strong-front and eddy-edge regions have enhanced ageostrophic shear and different attenuation than quiescent ones). Crucially, the std over the cell set is invariant to the (unknown) stencil cell ordering, so unlike explicit derivative features it carries zero layout risk, costs microseconds, and degrades gracefully at swath edges via the existing NaN→column-mean imputation.

I keep the verified gen006_03 skeleton (physics + stencil-spread features, ridge residualization, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, seed ensemble) and change one thing: checkpoint weight averaging. Each member currently restores the single best-validation checkpoint, which is a high-variance point estimate of an SGD trajectory bouncing around a noisy temporal-validation surface. Instead I retain the top-3 checkpoints by balanced validation MSE and average their weights (all from the same basin of the same run, so averaging is valid — the net is LayerNorm-based, no BatchNorm statistics to corrupt). This is a poor-man's SWA: it flattens the selected minimum, which is known to improve out-of-distribution/forward-in-time generalization — exactly what the temporally held-out test measures. A cheap guard re-evaluates the averaged weights on the validation tail and falls back to the single best checkpoint if averaging didn't help, so the change is strictly non-degrading up to one extra validation pass. Everything downstream (recency fine-tune, ensembling) is unchanged.

I keep the verified gen006_03 skeleton untouched (physics + stencil-spread features, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, seed ensemble — checkpoint averaging in gen007_00 bought nothing, so I drop it) and upgrade the deterministic baseline: after the closed-form linear ridge, I fit a random-Fourier-feature kernel ridge (2048 cos features at two RBF lengthscales, Gram matrix accumulated chunk-wise on the GPU, solved in float64 on CPU) on the linear residuals. This captures the smooth stationary-nonlinear part of the surface→subsurface map (e.g. saturating transfer, gentle regime bends) exactly and deterministically on all 1M rows — something the SGD-trained MLP must otherwise spend capacity and noisy gradients on. Per-component ridge strength is selected on the same temporal validation tail the MLP uses, with a strict guard: if no alpha beats the zero-prediction baseline on the tail, that component's RFF term is dropped, so the change is non-degrading by construction. The MLP then trains on the smaller post-kernel residual (Huber deltas and component weights recompute automatically), and its ensemble only has to model what a smooth kernel can't.

I build on the strongest verified program (gen006_03, 0.3290) rather than the weaker assigned parent, and make one focused change in the lineage's most reliably rewarded direction — a new layout-safe feature block: per-base-feature stencil validity fractions. After standardization, NaN stencil cells are imputed to 0 (the column mean), so the ridge and MLP currently cannot distinguish a genuinely mean-valued cell from an imputed one; swath-edge rows therefore look like artificially quiescent interior rows, biasing predictions toward the mean exactly where SWOT coverage degrades. For each of the 9 base features I append the fraction of finite cells across its 3x3 stencil (144 → 153 columns), computed before standardization. These missingness indicators are a classic, near-free win for mean-imputed models: the ridge can learn per-feature offsets/attenuation for partially observed rows, and the MLP can gate its residual correction on data quality. Like the stencil spread, the fraction is invariant to the unknown cell ordering (zero layout risk), never NaN itself, costs microseconds, and leaves every verified component (exact ridge + wind pseudo-stress + current-speed + spread features, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble) untouched.

I keep the verified gen007_02 skeleton (ridge residualization over physics + spread + validity features, component-balanced masked-Huber training, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, seed ensemble) and make one focused change in the lineage's most reliably rewarded direction — physics feature augmentation: relative-wind pseudo-stress. Ocean surface stress physically depends on the wind RELATIVE to the moving surface current, tau ~ rho*Cd*|W−Ug|(W−Ug), not the absolute wind; this "current feedback" (eddy-killing) effect is a documented O(10%) modulation of momentum flux that peaks exactly where currents are strong — the eddy/front regimes where the model's residual error concentrates. Per stencil cell I append |Wr|, |Wr|*wr_u, |Wr|*wr_v with Wr = (u10−ug, v10−vg) (153 → 180 columns). The cross terms |W−Ug|(W−Ug) contain wind-current coupling products (e.g. |W|·ug-type terms) that are NOT linear combinations of the existing absolute-stress and current-speed blocks, so both the closed-form ridge and the MLP gain a genuinely new, physically-correct forcing signal; the features are computed per-cell like the verified stress blocks, NaN-propagate to the standard column-mean imputation, and add negligible ridge/MLP cost.

I build on the strongest verified program (gen007_02, 0.3339) rather than the assigned parent (gen007_00's checkpoint averaging was verified neutral at 0.3290), and extend the lineage's single most reliably rewarded direction — physically-motivated quadratic speed features — to the one velocity pair still lacking them. Wind pseudo-stress (|W|·W) and total geostrophic current-speed (|Ug|·Ug) blocks each produced verified gains; the anomaly pair (ugosa, vgosa) still enters only linearly. Yet |Ua| is the eddy-intensity signal: mesoscale eddy kinetic energy is precisely the regime variable that sets how strongly surface geostrophic flow imprints on subsurface velocity (deep-reaching eddies vs shallow ephemeral anomalies), and drag/shear in the anomaly flow is quadratic just like in the mean flow. So per stencil cell I append |Ua|, |Ua|·ua, |Ua|·va for the ugosa/vgosa blocks (153 → 180 columns), computed before standardization so the exact ridge can use them directly — letting the linear stage represent eddy-strength-dependent attenuation/rotation of the anomaly current and shrinking the residual the MLP must learn. The change reuses the identical, twice-verified mechanism, is layout-safe under the known 81-column contract guard, costs milliseconds, and leaves every verified component (exact ridge residualization, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble, spread + validity features) untouched.

I build on the strongest verified program (gen007_02, 0.3339) and extend the lineage's most reliably rewarded direction — layout-safe stencil summary features — with the natural counterpart to gen007_02's validity fractions: a per-base-feature NaN-aware stencil MEAN (nanmean over the 9 cells, 153 → 162 columns). After standardization, NaN cells are imputed to 0, so any linear combination of a partially observed stencil is attenuated by the factor n_valid/9 — the imputed average equals the true local mean shrunk toward zero exactly at swath edges. The validity fraction told the models *how much* attenuation occurred; the nanmean supplies the *unattenuated* local estimate itself, which is the ratio of two existing quantities (imputed average / validity fraction) and thus not linearly recoverable by the ridge. For fully valid rows it is redundant-but-harmless; for edge rows it restores full-strength geostrophic and wind signal precisely where gen007_02 proved the headroom lives. Like spread and validity fraction it is ordering-invariant (zero layout risk), computed before standardization so the closed-form ridge uses it directly, and costs microseconds. Every verified component — exact ridge residualization, wind pseudo-stress + current-speed + spread + validity features, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble — is left untouched.

I keep the verified gen007_02 skeleton exactly (ridge residualization over physics + spread + validity features, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, 3-member seed ensemble) and make one focused change in the lineage's most reliably rewarded direction — physics feature augmentation — with a signal class not yet represented: wind–current interaction. Per stencil cell I append the dot product (u10·ug + v10·vg) and cross product (u10·vg − v10·ug) of the ERA5 wind and the geostrophic current (153 → 171 columns). These bilinear terms are genuinely new — the existing quadratic blocks are self-interactions of wind or current alone, so no linear combination of current features can express wind–current alignment — and they encode the dominant regime variable on the US West Coast: whether the wind blows with, against, or across the alongshore current, which sets upwelling-favorable Ekman transport, surface-layer shear, and hence how surface geostrophic velocity maps to subsurface velocity. Like every rewarded augmentation before it, the terms are per-cell, ordering-invariant across the layout, computed before standardization so the exact ridge sees them, and degrade gracefully to column-mean imputation at swath edges.

I build on the strongest verified program (gen007_02, 0.3339: validity fractions + spread + physics features over ridge residualization) rather than the assigned parent, and make one focused optimization change: exponential moving average (Polyak) weight averaging during the main training phase. SGD with a shared trunk on heavy-tailed residuals leaves noticeable step-to-step weight noise, and the current scheme checkpoints a single raw-SGD iterate chosen by validation — a high-variance selection. I maintain an EMA copy of the network (timm-style warmup decay ramping to 0.999), validate BOTH the raw and EMA weights each epoch, and checkpoint whichever is better, so the change is strictly a superset of the current selection and cannot select worse in-sample. Averaged iterates land in flatter regions of the loss surface, which is exactly what transfers across the temporal train→test shift this task scores on. The EMA update costs microseconds per step for a ~150k-parameter net, adds one cheap extra validation pass per epoch, and leaves every verified component (physics/spread/validity features, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, recency fine-tune from the selected weights, budgeted seed ensemble) untouched.

I keep the verified gen007_02 skeleton exactly (physics + spread + validity features, exact ridge residualization, component-balanced masked Huber with MSE-based selection, temporal validation, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble) and make one focused change: turn the homogeneous seed ensemble into an architecture-diverse ensemble. Members currently differ only by seed, so their errors are highly correlated and averaging cancels little variance — and the EMA attempt (gen008_03) showed that intra-trajectory averaging adds nothing here. Instead, member 0 keeps the verified (256,256,128)/0.1-dropout config with half the budget (so the ensemble always contains one full-strength known-good model), while members 1–2 use a wider (384,256,128)/0.15 net and a deeper-narrower (192,192,192,96)/0.05 net. Different widths/depths/regularization induce genuinely different inductive biases and decorrelated residual errors, which is exactly what makes ensemble averaging reduce the variance component of held-out error under the temporal train→test shift; every other verified component is untouched, so the downside is bounded by the diversity of two budget-limited members.

I keep the verified gen007_02 skeleton exactly (physics + spread + validity features, exact ridge residualization, component-balanced masked Huber trained / masked MSE selected, temporal tail validation, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble) and make one focused change: architectural diversity across ensemble members. I build on the strongest verified program (gen014_02, 0.3502 — the tail-fitted combine at gen015_02 and every other gen015 branch scored below it, so its blind equal-weight combine stands as validated) and push the lineage's one consistently verified gradient — recency — into the last place it is still diluted: the MLP recency fine-tune. The GBM's verified wins both came from a bounded recency window (most recent 500k valid rows), yet the MLP fine-tune sweeps the ENTIRE 1M-row span, so half of each low-LR pass drags the weights back toward the oldest cycles, and with only ~2 epochs the freshest rows get the same tiny exposure as data from a year before the test cycles. Now the fine-tune mirrors the trees' verified window: it trains only on the most recent 500k rows of the full span (oldest→newest within the window, same block-shuffled chronological sweep), and since each pass is half as long, the epoch cap rises to 4 inside the SAME reserved 20% time slice with the same deadline checks — so the fine-tune spends its unchanged budget entirely on the data closest in time to the held-out cycles instead of half-spending it on the stalest rows. Everything verified (physics/spread/validity features, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, EMA checkpointing, gated + recency-refit GBM, budgeted seed ensemble, equal-weight combine) is untouched.

I build on the strongest verified program (gen014_02, 0.3502) — every gen015/gen016 probe of the combine, the ridge, GBM capacity, and MLP architecture diversity lost ground, so the untouched weak spot is the MLP optimization schedule itself: ReduceLROnPlateau(patience=5) on members that only fit ~20–40 epochs inside their wall-clock slice typically fires zero or one decay, so each member's slice ends while it is still bouncing at a high learning rate, and both the raw checkpoint and the EMA inherit that SGD noise floor. I replace the plateau scheduler with a wall-clock-aware cosine annealing: each epoch the LR is set from the member's elapsed fraction of its own training slice, decaying 1e-3 → 2e-5 so every member — regardless of how many epochs its slice affords — is guaranteed to finish in a low-LR converged regime right when its budget expires. This is the classic budgeted-training schedule; it synergizes with the verified EMA checkpointing (EMA of a converging trajectory beats EMA of a noisy one) and needs no new hyperparameter search since the peak LR is unchanged. Everything else verified in this lineage (physics/spread/validity features, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, EMA, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble, gate-then-refit GBM) is byte-identical to gen014_02.

The parent's recency-blended ridge lost 0.022 against gen014_02 for two identifiable reasons: (i) after the tail gate selected a blend weight, the recent ridge was REFIT on a forward-shifted window and that unvalidated refit was deployed instead of the object the gate actually scored, and (ii) the blended ridge redefined the residual targets, which cascaded into the Huber deltas, the component weights, the GBM gating, and every MLP's training signal — a full-system shift disguised as one change. I keep the recency-ridge hypothesis but make it strictly additive and strictly validated: the residual stack (targets, deltas, weights, GBM, MLPs) is computed from the full-span ridge exactly as in the 0.3502 program, and the recent-window ridge enters ONLY as a prediction-time replacement of the linear term, per component, using precisely the blend that was scored on the untouched temporal tail (no post-gate refit), and only when it beats the full-span ridge there by a ≥1% MSE margin so noise-level wins can't flip the gate. With the materiality gate closed the program is byte-equivalent to gen014_02; when it opens, the deployed correction is exactly the validated one.

The parent carries this lineage's only untested regularizer — input-noise augmentation on the standardized training batches — but it never received the single biggest verified jump in the whole history: the decorrelated GBM residual member (+0.012 at gen014_01) with its recency refit (+0.005 at gen014_02). I graft exactly that verified component onto the parent: per target component, a HistGradientBoostingRegressor is fit on the RAW augmented features (NaNs intact, native missing handling — a fundamentally different treatment of swath-edge cells than the mean imputation the noise-trained MLPs see, so its errors decorrelate strongly), gated on the untouched temporal validation tail against the zero-residual predictor, and, only if it passes, refit on the most recent 500k valid rows of the full span so it also sees the freshest data before predicting test. The tree work gets the verified 26% wall-clock slice and the MLP members scale to the remaining time; everything the parent verified (physics/spread/validity features, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, clean-input validation, input-noise training, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble) is untouched. If input noise is additive with the tree member, this should land at or above the 0.3502 leader; the per-component gate bounds the downside at the parent's own ensemble.

The GBM residual member owns this lineage's largest verified gains (+0.012 inclusion, +0.005 recency refit), yet its boosting length is a blind constant: 100 iterations at lr 0.08 on 500k rows is almost certainly short of convergence, and nothing checks it either way. I raise the iteration ceiling to 160 and let the untouched temporal tail choose the actual tree count: the gate fit runs to the ceiling, staged_predict scores every intermediate stage on the tail (incremental, ~one full predict's cost), and the argmin stage n* both decides inclusion (best-stage MSE must beat ridge-alone, a strictly more generous but still tail-validated gate) and sets the iteration count for the verified full-span recency refit. If the clock is tight the gate model itself predicts test truncated at n* via staged_predict, so the fallback is never worse than today's fixed-100 model when 100 overshoots and is stronger when it undershoots. The GBM budget slice grows to 0.34 to cover the longer fits; the MLP slices already rescale to the remaining wall clock and their budgeted cosine schedule adapts to any slice length. Everything else verified (physics/spread/validity features, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, EMA checkpointing, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble) is untouched.

I port the one regularizer this champion lineage has never carried: Gaussian input-noise augmentation on the standardized training batches. Cross-lineage evidence says it works — gen016_03 (parent gen010_03) posts the board's best r2_v (0.4029) with input noise as its distinguishing ingredient, but from a weaker base it lands at 0.3483; grafting the same regularizer onto the strongest verified program (gen014_02, 0.3502) tests whether that v-side gain composes with the champion's stronger u side. Mechanistically it is a denoising regularizer well matched to this data: after standardization every NaN stencil cell is imputed to exactly 0.0, so the MLP can latch onto razor-thin decision structure around imputed values and onto instrument-level feature precision that does not persist across cycles; jittering each training batch with sigma=0.05 (in units of feature std) forces the learned correction to be locally smooth in feature space, which is precisely what transfers under the temporal distribution shift the held-out split measures. Noise is applied only in the main training loop — validation stays clean (selection must measure the true objective) and the recency fine-tune stays clean (its job is to absorb the freshest cycles' exact signal, which blurring would defeat). Everything else — plateau scheduler, EMA, ridge, physics/spread/validity features, component-balanced Huber, gate-then-refit GBM, budgeted seed ensemble — is byte-identical to gen014_02.

Every verified recency mechanism in this lineage (the MLP recency fine-tune, the GBM recency refit, +0.005 each) treats time-proximity to the test cycles as a bolt-on afterthought: the main MLP training epochs still weight a row from cycle 474 exactly like one from cycle 570. I bake recency into the entire training trajectory instead — each training row's loss contribution is scaled by a linear ramp from 0.5 (oldest row) to 1.5 (newest), normalized to mean 1 so the effective loss magnitude and tuned LR are unchanged. The weight is folded into the mask tensors used for training and the fine-tune sweep only; validation selection, GBM gating, the ridge, and the deltas all stay unweighted so selection remains clean and no verified component's statistics shift. Under temporal drift (seasonal winds, mesoscale regime changes) this tilts the whole optimization toward the distribution the held-out cycles are drawn from, rather than only the last two fine-tune epochs, and the modest 3:1 tilt keeps effective sample size high. Everything else in the parent (budgeted cosine LR, EMA checkpointing, gated+refit GBM, physics/spread/validity features, component-balanced masked Huber) is untouched.

Every recent probe of the combine weights, the GBM boosting budget, and recency weighting has landed at or below the 0.3502 champion — averaging is saturated because all four ensemble members (3 MLPs + GBM) independently learn the SAME post-ridge residual, so their errors stay correlated. I convert the GBM from a parallel averaged member into a boosting stage: per gated component, the pre-tail GBM's predictions on the full training span are subtracted from the residual targets, so the MLPs now learn the post-GBM residual — what the trees provably cannot capture — instead of competing to explain the same signal. The final prediction becomes ridge + gated GBM (recency refit, verified) + mean of MLPs, with no 1/(n+1) dilution of the tree contribution. The stack stays temporally clean: train/validation residuals are defined by the pre-tail GBM (which never saw the tail), so early stopping still measures forward-in-time generalization; Huber deltas and component-balance weights are recomputed on the post-GBM residuals so the loss geometry matches the new target. If a component's GBM fails its gate, that component reduces exactly to the parent's verified behavior. The GBM budget rises slightly (0.26 → 0.28) to cover the full-span train predict; everything else (physics/spread/validity features, exact ridge, cosine LR, EMA checkpointing, recency fine-tune, budgeted seed ensemble) is untouched.

Crossover repair: the parent's sole delta versus its lineage — a 0.6→1.4 recency ramp folded into the training masks for the whole optimization — is the largest measured regression on the board (0.3188 vs ~0.345 for the unweighted siblings; gen017_02/03 confirm continuous recency weighting keeps failing), while the GBM residual member is the largest verified gain (+0.012 inclusion, +0.005 recency refit in gen014_02, 0.3502). I therefore revert the training/fine-tune masks to pure validity masks — recency emphasis returns to its two verified discrete forms only (the low-LR oldest→newest fine-tune and the gated GBM recency refit) — and graft the champion's per-component, tail-gated, recency-refit HistGBM residual member into this parent. The one trait retained from the parent that the champion lacks is its warmup-ramped EMA (decay (1+s)/(10+s)→0.999 with LR steps on the min of raw/EMA validation), which avoids anchoring the weight average at the random init early in training; everything else verified in the lineage (physics/spread/validity augmentation, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal-tail validation, budgeted seed ensemble) is untouched.

Discrete recency keeps winning in this lineage (MLP recency fine-tune +0.005, GBM recency refit +0.005) while continuous recency weighting keeps losing (gen011_00, gen017_02/03), so I add a third discrete-recency mechanism at the ensemble level — cost-neutral and gated so it cannot dilute. The third seed member (which currently just adds a third full-span view on the smallest time slice) becomes a recent-window specialist: it trains on the most recent half of the pre-tail rows (a hard window, no sample weights), early-stops on the same untouched temporal tail, and runs its verified oldest→newest fine-tune over the recent half of the full span. Because a half-data same-family member is weaker than the GBM's decorrelated family, its inclusion gate is stricter than the GBM's beats-zero test: it joins the equal-weight average only if it also lands within 5% of the best full-span member's tail validation loss; otherwise the ensemble reverts exactly to the champion's two full members + GBM. Everything else verified in gen014_02 (physics/spread/validity augmentation, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, EMA checkpointing, gate-then-refit GBM) is untouched.

Ensemble diversity is the single biggest verified gain in this lineage (the decorrelated GBM family, +0.012), yet the three MLP members are architecturally identical clones differing only by seed — their errors are highly correlated, so averaging them buys little variance reduction. I extend the verified decorrelation mechanism to the MLP slice: member 0 keeps the exact verified architecture (256, 256, 128) so the ensemble always contains one full-strength known-good model, while member 1 becomes wider-and-shallower (384, 192) and member 2 deeper-and-narrower (192, 192, 192, 96). Different depths/widths induce different inductive biases (smoother vs. more compositional fits of the residual), decorrelating member errors far more than seed noise does, while parameter counts stay within ~15% of the original so per-epoch cost and the 4 GB memory envelope are unchanged. Each member is still validation-checkpointed on the temporal tail with the EMA candidate, so a weaker architecture cannot dilute much — it ships its best-found weights or is dominated by its own early-stopped state. Everything verified (physics/spread/validity features, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, budgeted cosine LR, EMA checkpointing, recency fine-tune, gated+recency-refit GBM, combine weights) is untouched.

Ensemble diversity is the only lever with large verified gains in this lineage (the decorrelated GBM family +0.012, architecture-diverse MLPs +0.003 on top of the previous champion), and gen018_02 applied it to the MLP side — but the tree side is still a single model per component. I add a second, deliberately diverse GBM family: deeper trees (127 leaves), stronger shrinkage (lr 0.12, 70 iters, l2 2.0, min_samples_leaf 80), AND a different data view — every 2nd row of the last 1M valid rows, so it sees twice the time span at the same row count. Each family independently runs the verified gate-then-refit protocol (gated on the untouched temporal tail against the zero-residual predictor, then recency-refit on the full span), and the included families are AVERAGED into the single tree member, so the verified MLP:tree combine ratio is untouched and a failed family dilutes nothing. Family A (the exact verified config) runs completely first for both components, so under a tight clock the program degrades to exactly the parent; the tree budget cap rises to 0.38 of the wall clock, but since the MLP slices scale to the actual remaining time, any unused tree budget flows straight back to the MLPs. Everything else — physics/spread/validity features, exact ridge, component-balanced masked Huber, temporal validation, EMA checkpointing, budgeted cosine LR, recency fine-tune, architecture-diverse MLP ensemble — is byte-identical to the parent.

I merge the two verified gen018 gains (architecture-diverse MLPs from the parent plus the diverse GBM families, +0.004 in gen018_03) and extend the diversity lever — the only one with large verified gains in this lineage — along a third, still-unexplored axis: TARGET space. MLP member 2 now trains on the post-ridge residuals rotated 45° in the (u, v) plane, predicting (u+v)/√2 and (v−u)/√2; its predictions are rotated back before averaging. A rotated-basis learner splits capacity and errors along different physical axes (roughly along/across-shore for USWC), so its per-component errors decorrelate from the axis-aligned members and the tree family in a way seed or architecture changes cannot; velocity is a vector field, so a coordinate rotation is exactly as physical as the original basis. Rotated targets need both components valid, so the member gets its own joint mask and its own rotated Huber deltas/component weights; if fewer than 100k joint-valid rows exist it silently falls back to the unrotated targets, and members 0–1, the tree side, the combine, and every verified mechanism (ridge, EMA, budgeted cosine LR, recency fine-tune, gate-then-refit) are byte-identical — a failed rotation dilutes at most one quarter of the residual correction and costs zero extra time.

I build on the champion gen019_00 (all its verified mechanisms untouched) and attack the one axis every generation has left at its default: the COMBINE. The ensemble now has four members (three diverse MLPs, one averaged tree family) that are always averaged with equal weights per component, yet their quality is measurably unequal per component (trees earned +0.012 alone; the rotated/deeper members are deliberately weaker fits). I replace the uniform average with tail-stacked weights: each MLP's selected pre-fine-tune checkpoint (trained strictly before the tail) and each gated pre-tail GBM predicts the temporal validation tail, and per component a non-negative least squares fit on those leak-free tail predictions learns the member weights, which are then shrunk 50% toward uniform and applied to the recency-refit test predictions. NNLS on a held-out later-in-time tail directly optimizes the forward-in-time criterion the score measures, down-weights whichever member happens to be weak for that component, and its unconstrained sum doubles as a variance-calibrating shrinkage that MSE/R^2 rewards; the 50% shrink plus finiteness/sum guards bound the tail-overfit risk, and any failure falls back to the exact gen019_00 equal-weight combine.

Every model in this lineage — the MLPs, the GBM families, the combine — fits the RESIDUAL of a ridge whose regularization has been frozen at alpha=10 since it was introduced, even as the feature space grew from 81 to 153 columns of very different SNR (raw stencil cells vs. quadratic stress products vs. spread/validity summaries). I keep every verified mechanism of the parent untouched and tune only the ridge backbone: per component, the Gram/moment statistics are accumulated separately over the pre-tail span and the temporal tail, a 6-point alpha grid (1..300, containing the verified 10) is solved from the pre-tail statistics alone and scored on the untouched tail — the exact forward-in-time criterion the harness measures — and the winning alpha is then refit in closed form on the full span by simply summing the two statistic blocks, so no data is wasted. A better-shrunk linear backbone shifts variance out of the residual that the noisy SGD/tree members must otherwise model, which should lift both components; risk is negligible because alpha=10 stays in the grid, selection uses ~100k tail rows against only 6 candidates, and the added cost is one extra tail Gram accumulation (~10% of the ridge step).

I extend the single most-verified lever in this lineage — decorrelated GBM families (+0.012 in gen014_01, +0.004 in gen018_03) — along a still-unexplored diversity axis: the LOSS FUNCTION. A third tree family fits the post-ridge residuals with loss="absolute_error" (median regression) on a stride-3 window covering the longest time span yet (~1.5M rows of history at the same row count). Every existing member — ridge, MLPs, both GBM families — minimizes a squared/Huber-quadratic objective, so their errors share the same sensitivity to the heavy-tailed HFR noise; an L1-fit family has a genuinely different loss geometry (fits the conditional median, immune to tail outliers) and a third data view, decorrelating its errors in a way hyperparameter or stride changes cannot. Risk is near zero by construction: the family runs last inside the unchanged GBM wall-clock cap (skipped under a tight clock), the verified gate-then-refit protocol rejects it per component unless it beats ridge-alone tail MSE — the metric's own currency, so a median-bias that hurts MSE cannot get in — and the tail-stacked NNLS combine then weights the averaged tree member by measured tail skill. Families 0–1, all MLP members, the stacking, and every other verified mechanism are byte-identical to the champion.

I merge the two verified gen019 gains, which act at opposite ends of the pipeline and therefore should compose additively: the parent's tail-tuned ridge backbone (per-component alpha selected on the temporal tail, +0.0003 over gen018_03) keeps every downstream member fitting the smallest possible residual, and the champion gen019_01's tail-stacked combine (+0.0005 over gen019_00) replaces the one remaining default — the equal-weight member average — with per-component non-negative least squares weights learned on leak-free tail predictions (each MLP's selected pre-fine-tune checkpoint, which never trained on the tail, and the gated pre-tail GBM fits). NNLS on the later-in-time tail directly optimizes the forward-in-time criterion the harness scores, down-weights whichever member is weak for that component, and its unconstrained weight sum acts as a variance-calibrating shrinkage of the residual correction; the fitted weights are shrunk 50% toward uniform and guarded on tail size, finiteness, and weight sum, falling back to the parent's exact equal-weight combine on any failure — so the candidate cannot lose either parent's verified behavior, only reweight it.

The parent's single verified tree family is the one member every stronger sibling has since upgraded: decorrelated GBM families are the most-verified lever in this lineage (+0.012 in gen014_01, +0.004 more in gen018_03, carried into every champion). I graft exactly that change into this parent, leaving its recency-weighted MLP training untouched: a second tree family that is diverse along two axes at once — a different function class (deeper 127-leaf trees, stronger shrinkage 0.12, heavier L2) and a different data view (stride-2 window covering twice the time span at the same row count). Each family runs the parent's verified gate-then-refit protocol independently against the untouched temporal tail, so a family that fails the gate dilutes nothing, and the included families are averaged into the single tree ensemble member the combine already expects. The GBM deadline rises from 0.26 to 0.38 of the budget, but it is a deadline, not a reservation — the MLP slices are computed from time actually remaining, so unused tree time flows back to the MLPs. Averaging two differently-biased, differently-windowed tree fits reduces the variance of the residual correction on later cycles, which is precisely what the forward-in-time R^2 rewards.

The tail-stacked combine (verified +0.0005 in this parent) opened a new interface: any leak-free tail predictor can now join the ensemble at whatever weight the temporal tail says it deserves, with zero risk to the champion combine. I use that interface to attack the one term every generation has held frozen: the ridge baseline itself, which is fit on the full training span with uniform weight even though the test split is strictly later in time and the task statement says temporal generalization is what scores. I add a RECENCY-RIDGE DRIFT member: a second closed-form ridge fit only on the most recent 400k pre-tail rows; its prediction MINUS the full ridge's is a direct estimate of coefficient/intercept drift (seasonal wind-regime shifts, mean-flow drift) and enters the NNLS stack as one extra column whose uniform-prior weight is ZERO — so per component the tail data alone decides how much drift correction to apply, and every fallback path reduces byte-for-byte to the parent's combine. For the test prediction the drift ridge is recency-refit on the last 400k rows of the full span (the verified gate/refit protocol). Cost is two chunked closed-form ridge solves (~seconds), taking no time from any member.

I keep every verified mechanism of the champion gen020_02 (which builds on this same parent: architecture/rotation-diverse MLPs, diverse gated GBM families, tail-stacked NNLS combine, recency-ridge drift column) and make one change on the lineage's most repeatedly verified axis — physics feature augmentation (stress terms, current-speed terms, stencil spread, validity fractions were each separate verified gains). I add WIND–CURRENT COUPLING features: per stencil cell, |W|·ug and |W|·vg. Physically, wind speed sets mixed-layer depth and vertical momentum mixing, which gates how strongly the surface geostrophic current imprints on the subsurface: strong-wind (deep-mixing) regimes couple surface to subsurface currents, calm stratified regimes decouple them. Neither existing block spans this — the stress block is wind-only, the current block is current-only — so the closed-form ridge currently cannot represent wind-modulated attenuation of the geostrophic transfer at all, and the MLP/GBM must synthesize the product themselves. Adding the 18 columns (153→171) hands this leading-order interaction to every member, including the ridge baseline and both drift ridges, at negligible cost (~100 MB RAM, trivial solve-time growth).
